title: Checkout API: what the new index changed, and where to keep sessions
summary: Two blocks that show numbers: the measures before and after the change, and a weighted comparison of the session store options. Example data for a performance review.

blocks.title: Why
blocks.text: The checkout endpoint scanned the whole `orders` table on every call. This change adds a partial index on open orders and moves session reads off the database. The first block shows the numbers from the benchmark run on `main` and on this branch. The second compares the places sessions could live, so the store can be decided before the PR merges.

blocks.title: Checkout API, main vs this PR

measures.title: p95 latency
measures.detail: The partial index on `orders(status) WHERE status = 'open'` replaces the sequential scan. The trend is the last six nightly runs; the drop is this branch.

measures.title: Client bundle
measures.detail: The session client adds 4.1 KB. Under the 2% budget, over the 0.5% warning line.

measures.title: Peak memory
measures.detail: The session cache holds up to 40 MB. It is bounded, and the pod limit is 1 GB, so this is accepted for now. The store question below decides whether it stays.

measures.title: Cart totals
measures.detail: Sessions no longer join through `orders`, so this case gains from the store change, not the index.

criteria.title: Operational cost
criteria.detail: What the team has to run, watch and upgrade. Weighted highest: the team is three people.

criteria.title: Migration risk
criteria.detail: How much can go wrong moving the 2 million live sessions.

scores.reason: A new cluster to run and page on.
Sessions are lost on every deploy.

questions.prompt: Where should sessions live after this change?

options.title: A Postgres table
options.detail: Same database, an unlogged table with a TTL sweep.

options.title: Redis
options.detail: Fastest reads, but a new service to run.

options.title: In process memory
options.detail: No new parts; sessions do not survive a deploy.
